strengths: Addresses a relevant and practical indoor localization setting where floorplans are lightweight and persistent compared with full 3D maps or image databases.
The method is technically coherent: heteroscedastic Laplace floorplan-depth prediction is cleanly integrated into an observation likelihood and histogram filter.
Empirical results are strong on the reported benchmarks, especially LaMAR HGE, with large gains over F3Loc for sequential localization and shorter trajectories.
The paper includes useful ablations separating pretrained depth encoders from uncertainty modeling, plus comparisons across several encoders and runtime measurements.
Supplementary experiments add cross-building transfer, update-frequency, and grid-resolution analyses, which help support the robustness and efficiency story.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core ingredients are a pretrained monocular-depth encoder, heteroscedastic uncertainty regression, and a histogram filter closely related to prior F3Loc machinery.

The claimed scalability/generalization is somewhat overstated because the model is still trained on floorplan-depth supervision for the target dataset in most experiments; the main cross-building evidence is small, with only N=2 sequences for T=100 in Table 3.
Evaluation depends heavily on a reimplementation of F3Loc for LaMAR, and stronger or more diverse baselines for real-world localization are limited; F3Loc fusion is not evaluated on LaMAR.

Several practical assumptions are underexplored, including accurate relative poses/odometry, gravity, intrinsics, and manually modified floorplans. Robustness to noise in these inputs and to floorplan inaccuracies is not sufficiently tested.
The uncertainty estimates are only evaluated indirectly through localization; calibration, failure cases, and whether uncertainties are statistically meaningful are not analyzed.
Runtime on the large LaMAR floorplan is close to one second per frame for matching plus extraction, so the real-time/practical deployment claims need more careful qualification.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: indoor localization from floorplans, where compact, persistent map representations are practically appealing compared with full 3D reconstruction or image databases.
The proposed pipeline is technically coherent, combining gravity alignment, floorplan-depth prediction, an uncertainty-aware Laplace observation model, and histogram filtering.
The evaluation includes both synthetic and real-world datasets, and the reported results show clear improvements over F3Loc in several settings, especially on LaMAR HGE and shorter sequences.
The ablations separating pretrained encoders, uncertainty modeling, and encoder choice are useful and indicate that uncertainty can improve sequential filtering.
weaknesses: The central claim of avoiding per-environment or per-dataset depth training is overstated. Although the encoder is pretrained, the method still trains a prediction head on dataset-specific floorplan-depth supervision, including 50 epochs on the respective dataset. This substantially weakens the claimed deployment advantage over F3Loc.

Novelty is limited. The method is largely an incremental combination of a stronger pretrained monocular-depth encoder with an uncertainty output and a standard Bayesian/histogram filter. The uncertainty model is a straightforward Laplace likelihood, and the paper does not convincingly establish it as a major conceptual advance.

The evaluation is not sufficiently convincing for a top-tier acceptance. Several key real-world results rely on very small numbers of test sequences, e.g. LaMAR HGE has only 11 sequences at T=100 and the CAB cross-building test has only 2 sequences at T=100. This makes the large multiplicative improvement claims fragile.

The strongest gains appear to come primarily from replacing F3Loc's depth network with a modern pretrained depth encoder, not from the proposed uncertainty modeling. On single-frame localization, uncertainty sometimes slightly hurts performance, and even in sequential results the no-uncertainty variant is already strong.

The generalization evidence is weak. The CAB experiment is not a true zero-shot setting by the authors' own admission, uses the same sensor ecosystem, has very few sequences, and still shows poor performance for shorter trajectories. Fine-tuning is needed for better results, which undercuts the scalability narrative.

Important baselines and comparisons are incomplete. F3Loc fusion is not evaluated on LaMAR, and broader modern localization alternatives are mostly absent from the main empirical comparison. The paper relies heavily on one prior method as the main competitor.

The uncertainty estimates are not evaluated as uncertainties. There is no calibration analysis, negative log-likelihood comparison, reliability diagram, correlation between predicted uncertainty and error, or study of failure cases where uncertainty specifically prevents filter collapse.

Some practical claims are overstated. Runtime on LaMAR is close to one second per frame, dominated by matching, yet the paper describes the method as real-time or efficient without enough system-level evidence. The dependence on gravity, intrinsics, relative poses, manual floorplan modifications, and occupancy-map quality is also under-discussed.

Absolute localization performance remains limited in challenging real-world settings. For LaMAR single-frame localization, recall is low even at loose thresholds, and GT-depth upper bounds are also surprisingly poor, suggesting unresolved issues with floorplan representation, map alignment, or evaluation setup.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a paper making strong empirical claims. The manuscript gives high-level training settings but lacks enough detail about data preprocessing, manual floorplan edits, sequence sampling, model architecture dimensions, uncertainty constraints, hyperparameter selection, and whether code/models will be released.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical localization setting: RGB-based indoor localization against lightweight floorplans, avoiding the storage and maintenance costs of image databases or 3D maps.
The core idea of using uncertainty-aware floorplan depth predictions inside a histogram filter is well motivated, technically clean, and directly targets a clear weakness of F3Loc.

Empirical results are strong across Gibson, Structured3D, and especially LaMAR HGE, with large gains over F3Loc in sequential localization and consistent benefits from uncertainty modeling in harder real-world cases.

The ablations are useful: the paper separates the effects of stronger pretrained depth encoders from uncertainty modeling, evaluates several encoder choices, includes single-frame and sequential settings, and reports runtime tradeoffs.
The method is presented clearly, with understandable probabilistic modeling and good qualitative visualizations of depth predictions, likelihoods, and posterior evolution.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental: the pipeline remains close to F3Loc, with the main changes being a pretrained depth encoder and Laplace uncertainty prediction. This is valuable, but not a major conceptual departure.

The claim of avoiding per-environment or per-dataset depth training is overstated. Although the encoder is pretrained, the method still trains the masked attention/depth-uncertainty head on dataset-specific floorplan depth supervision for 50 epochs, including LaMAR HGE.
The real-world evaluation has small sequence counts for several key settings, especially LaMAR HGE at T=100 with N=11 and CAB with N=2, making some headline gains statistically fragile.

The comparison to F3Loc on LaMAR depends on the authors' retraining and custom preprocessing/floorplan modifications, so the very large performance gap could partly reflect implementation, tuning, or data-processing differences rather than only the proposed modeling changes.

Runtime on large real-world floorplans is relatively high, around one second per frame on LaMAR, and the claim of efficient or real-time operation is only partially supported; the supplementary coarser-grid experiments help but also show accuracy degradation.

Generalization evidence is promising but limited: the CAB transfer experiment is small, uses the same sensor family, and the supplementary results indicate that target-domain fine-tuning is still helpful for optimal performance.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practical indoor localization setting: localizing RGB image sequences against lightweight floorplans, avoiding heavy 3D maps or image databases.

The proposed probabilistic formulation is clean and well integrated into the histogram filter: floorplan depth is modeled with a Laplace likelihood whose scale is predicted uncertainty, and the same uncertainty is used in local trajectory refinement.
The evaluation shows large empirical gains over F3Loc on both synthetic Gibson and real LaMAR HGE/CAB settings, especially for short sequences where rapid convergence matters.

Ablations are useful: the paper separates the effect of stronger pretrained depth encoders, uncertainty modeling, post-processing, encoder choice, Gaussian vs Laplace uncertainty, update frequency, and grid resolution.
The method has a practical flavor: it uses occupancy-only floorplans, gravity alignment, off-the-shelf monocular depth encoders, and reports runtime and large-floorplan considerations.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. Much of the gain appears to come from replacing F3Loc's depth backbone with Depth Anything v2 and adding a fairly standard aleatoric uncertainty likelihood; the core filtering setup remains close to F3Loc.

The paper's claim of eliminating per-environment depth training is somewhat overstated. Although the encoder is pretrained, the method still trains a depth/uncertainty prediction head on dataset-specific floorplan-depth supervision, and the appendix reports training on each dataset for 50 epochs.

The real-world evaluation has small sequence counts for the most important LaMAR settings, e.g. only 11 trajectories for T=100, making some headline percentage and fold-improvement claims statistically fragile.

The LaMAR floorplan/pose alignment involves manual modifications and manually selected doorway correspondences, with no independent 2D pose ground truth. This weakens the strength of the real-world evidence and may make reproduction difficult.

The comparison to baselines is not entirely complete: F3Loc fusion is not evaluated on LaMAR, other recent map/floorplan localization methods are mostly copied from prior work or absent, and the post-processing step is not applied symmetrically to baselines.

Some results are hard to interpret, such as post-processing exceeding the GT-depth upper bound on Gibson short sequences, suggesting the evaluation protocol or upper-bound framing needs clearer explanation.

Runtime is less compelling than the text suggests for large floorplans: LaMAR matching plus feature extraction is around one second per frame, with additional end-of-sequence post-processing, so the real-time claim is only conditionally supported.
Reproducibility is promised but the extracted manuscript leaves the code/materials URL blank, and important preprocessing choices for floorplans are manual.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practical problem: indoor localization from RGB sequences and floorplans, where avoiding dense 3D maps is attractive.
The proposed system is coherent and combines pretrained depth features, uncertainty-aware likelihoods, histogram filtering, and a local trajectory refinement in a reasonable way.

The empirical results show clear gains over F3Loc on the reported benchmarks, especially on short sequences in LaMAR HGE, and the paper includes several useful ablations over encoder choice, uncertainty distribution, update frequency, and grid resolution.
The use of an off-the-shelf depth foundation model is a sensible engineering direction and appears to improve robustness relative to the custom depth predictor used in prior work.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. Much of the improvement appears to come from replacing the prior depth network with Depth Anything v2 and adding a fairly standard Laplace aleatoric uncertainty loss/likelihood, rather than from a fundamentally new localization method.

The main claims about avoiding per-environment or per-dataset training are overstated. The method still trains a masked attention head for 50 epochs on dataset-specific floorplan-depth labels, and the LaMAR setup requires manual floorplan modifications and manual alignment of 6-DoF trajectories to 2D floorplans.

The uncertainty modeling is not evaluated as uncertainty. There are no calibration curves, error-uncertainty correlations, NLL comparisons, or analysis showing that predicted uncertainties are statistically meaningful; the paper only reports downstream localization gains.

The evaluation is narrow and heavily centered on F3Loc. Comparisons to broader localization, retrieval, SLAM, or map-based baselines are missing or superficial, and the strongest real-world claims depend on a baseline retrained by the authors whose performance is extremely poor on LaMAR.

The real-world evaluation has small effective test counts in several settings, e.g. only 11 length-100 HGE sequences and very few CAB sequences, making the large multiplicative improvement claims fragile.

The post-processing refinement substantially contributes to the headline numbers and can even exceed the reported GT-depth upper bound, which makes the interpretation of the tables confusing and weakens the claimed causal role of uncertainty-aware filtering.

The LaMAR ground truth construction is concerning: the paper admits there is no independent 2D pose ground truth, uses manually selected doorway correspondences, and modifies floorplans. This introduces possible bias and limits confidence in the real-world quantitative results.

The practical efficiency claims are not fully convincing. On the large LaMAR floorplan, matching alone is around 0.88 seconds per frame, plus about 0.96 seconds for post-processing, which is hard to reconcile with real-time AR or robotics deployment.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript as provided: the code/materials link appears blank, and important implementation choices such as architecture details, ray counts, discretization, optimizer settings for post-processing, and hyperparameters are not sufficiently specified in the main text.
Overall, the paper is plausible and has positive empirical signals, but the contribution is too incremental and the evidence too entangled and fragile for a top-tier AI acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical localization setting: indoor SE(2) localization from RGB sequences and readily available floorplans, avoiding heavy 3D maps or image databases.

The core formulation is clean and well motivated: predicting per-ray floorplan depth with heteroscedastic uncertainty and using a Laplace likelihood inside a histogram filter is technically sensible and integrates naturally with sequential Bayesian localization.
Empirical results are strong, especially on challenging real-world LaMAR HGE sequences and short sequence lengths; the reported gains over F3Loc are large and relevant for practical time-to-localize.

The paper includes useful ablations isolating the effect of pretrained depth encoders, uncertainty modeling, post-processing, model size/runtime tradeoffs, grid resolution, update frequency, and Laplace vs Gaussian uncertainty.
Presentation is generally clear, with enough implementation and dataset-processing detail to understand and reproduce the approach in principle.
weaknesses: The novelty is more incremental than foundational: the method largely combines a stronger pretrained depth encoder, heteroscedastic depth prediction, Laplace likelihood matching, and an existing histogram-filter localization framework.

The claim of avoiding environment-specific training is somewhat overstated. While the depth backbone is pretrained, the floorplan-depth/uncertainty prediction head is still trained on dataset-specific floorplan-depth labels, including LaMAR training sessions.

Some key real-world evaluations are small: for example, LaMAR HGE has only 11 length-100 test sequences, and the cross-building CAB sequential result has very few long sequences, making the strongest numerical claims somewhat statistically fragile.

The method depends on accurate gravity, intrinsics, ego-motion, floorplans, and manual floorplan/pose alignment choices; these assumptions and preprocessing steps may limit deployment robustness more than the main text emphasizes.
Runtime on large real floorplans is close to or above one second per frame plus post-processing, so the real-time claim is plausible only under reduced update rates or lower frame-rate use cases.

The comparison set is centered mainly on F3Loc and its variants; broader comparisons to modern retrieval/localization pipelines or alternative uncertainty/filtering baselines would strengthen the positioning.
